extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examiners on performing the §101 patent eligibility analysis under MPEP §2106, including Step 1 (statutory category) and Step 2A (Alice/Mayo two-prong test) determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 1: Whether a claim is to a statutory category
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1 of the eligibility analysis asks: Is the claim to a process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should be made after determining what applicant has invented by reviewing the entire application disclosure and construing the claims in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI). In the flowchart Step 1 determines whether the claim as a whole does not fall within any statutory category (Step 1: NO) and thus is non-statutory (warranting rejection), or falls within one or more statutory categories (Step 1: YES) and must be further analyzed (Pathway A or Step 2A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction and review of the disclosure before eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine what applicant has invented by reviewing the entire application disclosure and construing the claims in accordance with their broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2106 subsection II and MPEP §2111 for more information about the importance of understanding what the applicant has invented and the BRI. Eligibility evaluation should be made after this determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims whose BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments fail Step 1
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim whose BRI covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims fail Step 1 (Step 1: NO) and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. Best practice: examiner should point out the BRI and recommend an amendment, if possible, to narrow the claim to statutory embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitory signals and machine-readable media may be non-statutory embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitory, propagating signals do not fall within any statutory category; machine-readable media BRI can encompass non-statutory transitory forms (e.g., carrier waves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a computer-readable medium claim that can be a compact disc or a carrier wave covers a non-statutory embodiment and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101. See In re Nuijten and Mentor Graphics v. EVE-USA decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating Step 1 rejections and recommending amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is clearly not within one of the four categories (Step 1: NO), a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 for such rejections (see MPEP §2106.07(a)(1)). If the claim fails Step 1 but applicant’s disclosure suggests an amendable claim could fall within a statutory category, proceed to determine eligibility of a proposed amendment and recommend amendment as a best practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 2A: Whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A asks: Is the claim directed to a law of nature, a natural phenomenon (product of nature) or an abstract idea?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a claim falls within a statutory category, it may still be ineligible if it is directed to only abstract ideas, natural phenomena, or laws of nature. If Step 2A: NO the claim is not directed to a judicial exception and is eligible at Pathway B; if Step 2A: YES the claim is directed to a judicial exception and requires Step 2B analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions and the underlying concern of preemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicially recognized exceptions: abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena (also described as physical phenomena, products of nature, scientific principles, mental processes, disembodied mathematical algorithms, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court explains these exceptions are 'basic tools of scientific and technological work' and are excluded because monopolization might impede innovation; preemption is the concern underlying the exceptions. Preemption, however, is not a standalone test and is addressed through the Alice/Mayo two-part framework (Steps 2A and 2B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A two-prong inquiry: Prong One — does the claim recite a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong One asks whether the claim recites (sets forth or describes) an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Set forth’ and ‘described’ are both equated with ‘recite’ but indicate two ways exceptions appear in claims (explicitly stated vs. described conceptually). Examiners must distinguish claims that recite an exception (require further analysis) from claims that merely involve an exception (eligible). Examples: 'A machine comprising elements that operate in accordance with F=ma' recites a law of nature; a teeter-totter claim that merely involves lever principles does not recite the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A two-prong inquiry: Prong Two — integration of the exception into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Prong Two asks whether the claim recites additional elements that integrate the judicial exception into a practical application of that exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the additional elements integrate the exception into a practical application, the claim is not directed to the judicial exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible at Pathway B. If the additional elements do not integrate the exception into a practical application, the claim is directed to the exception (Step 2A: YES) and requires Step 2B analysis. See MPEP §2106.04(d)(2) for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency of mere additional elements that are also judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are no additional claim elements besides the judicial exception, or if the additional claim elements merely recite another judicial exception, that is insufficient to integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding one abstract idea to another does not render a claim non-abstract (RecogniCorp v. Nintendo). For eligibility, additional elements must 'transform the nature of the claim' into a patent-eligible application (Alice). If no sufficient additional elements exist, recommend amendment if possible and make appropriate §101 rejection (see MPEP §2106.07).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating claims reciting multiple judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may recite multiple judicial exceptions; the eligibility analysis should be applied the same regardless of the number of exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless clear that exceptions are distinct (e.g., a law of nature and an abstract idea), avoid parsing the claim into multiple exceptions. If distinct, select one exception for efficiency and analyze it; if analysis shows additional elements integrate or amount to significantly more than the selected exception, consider the claim eligible. If multiple abstract ideas or laws of nature are recited together, treat them together for Prong Two and Step 2B where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated groupings of abstract ideas for examiner identification
rubrics_metrics.description: To facilitate examination, MPEP distills case law into enumerated groupings of abstract ideas: (1) Mathematical concepts; (2) Certain methods of organizing human activity; (3) Mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group 1: mathematical relationships, formulas, calculations. Group 2: fundamental economic principles/practices (hedging, insurance), commercial/legal interactions (contracts, advertising, marketing), managing personal behavior/relationships, social activities, teaching, following rules. Group 3: concepts performed in the human mind (observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion). See MPEP §2106.04(a)(2) for more discussion and relationships to case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for identifying abstract idea limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea by (1) identifying the specific limitation(s) in the claim that the examiner believes recites an abstract idea, and (2) determining whether those limitations fall within at least one enumerated grouping of abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the identified limitation(s) falls within a grouping, conclude the claim recites an abstract idea and proceed to Prong Two. If not, conclude the claim does not recite an abstract idea and the abstract idea exception analysis concludes, except in rare circumstances (see MPEP §2106.04(a)(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty of a judicial exception does not affect exception status
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial exceptions need not be old or long-prevalent; newly discovered or novel judicial exceptions are still exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The courts have held that novelty of the underlying concept (e.g., a newly discovered law of nature or mathematical formula) does not make it patent-eligible; the concern is tying up the use of such tools (Myriad, Mayo, Flook). The novelty of an exception is not a determinative factor in §101 analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption is a concern but not a standalone test
rubrics_metrics.description: Although preemption is the policy concern underlying the judicial exceptions, the absence or presence of preemption itself is not the sole test for eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions of preemption are inherent in and resolved by applying the Alice/Mayo two-part framework (Steps 2A and 2B). A claim may be eligible despite not completely avoiding preemption in some narrow senses, and absence of complete preemption does not by itself demonstrate eligibility.
